title: Am I right?
opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
prayer: Lord, you have searched me and you know me. Show me the places where judgment, resentment, pride, or comfort have made me blind. Help me recognize the people you place before me. Give me wisdom to know when to speak, when to listen, when to help, when to forgive, and when simply to remain beside someone in love. I cannot repair everything that is broken, Lord, but I can respond to what you place before me today. Let my life make it easier, not harder, for another person to find you. Amen.
body:
Some readings are familiar enough that we think we already know what they are going to say. But today, Corinthians, Psalm 139, and the Gospel of John seem to ask something much more uncomfortable.

“Knowledge inflates with pride, but love builds up.”

It is easy to understand love when the person standing before us is easy to love. It becomes something entirely different when someone has offended us, disappointed us, taken something from us, or simply lives in a way we do not understand.

It is easy to judge the thief. It is harder to examine ourselves and ask whether we are giving as generously as we could. It is easy to notice those who have more than they need while overlooking those in need because, after all, there will always be someone in need. It is easy to continue wanting more while forgetting what an extraordinary blessing it is simply to wake up, walk into a kitchen, and cook breakfast every morning.

And it is very easy to walk away from someone who has hurt us.

Sometimes the hurt remains long after the person is gone. We replay what happened. Anger becomes resentment, resentment can become hatred, and somehow the person who hurt us continues occupying space within us even though we no longer want anything to do with them.

Forgiveness does not mean pretending the wrong was acceptable. It does not necessarily mean restoring the relationship. Boundaries can still be necessary. 

Then Paul introduces something even harder. The Corinthians knew that meat sacrificed to idols was simply meat because an idol had no real power. Yet Paul warns them that their behavior could still lead someone with a weaker understanding into sin. Their argument might have been: I know better, so what I do shouldn't matter.

Paul says it does matter.

The question is no longer simply, Am I right?

The question becomes, Does the way I am living help another person toward God, or make it harder for them to find him?

That reaches directly into our own families.

Our children grow up and make decisions we would never make for them. They may not share our faith. They may choose things we dislike or believe are wrong. We can tell them what we believe. We can guide them. But eventually we have to ask ourselves another difficult question: Will they encounter the God I love through the way I love them, or will they primarily remember my disapproval?**

We do not have to approve of everything someone does in order to love them.

Perhaps that is precisely where love becomes Christian love.

The same question appears everywhere. When someone is frightened, confused, pregnant, poor, lonely, addicted, grieving, angry, or making a decision we believe is wrong, it can be easier to separate ourselves from the situation. We tell ourselves that it is their life, their decision, their problem.

Sometimes respecting another person's freedom is necessary. But love may still ask something of us: to listen, to speak, to offer help, to show someone resources they did not know existed, to correct gently when appropriate, or simply to remain beside them while they struggle.

But then another problem appears.

There is so much suffering.

There are always people who need something. There will always be injustice, poverty, broken relationships, difficult children, lonely people and people making terrible decisions. If Christian love requires us to respond to everything, the responsibility becomes so enormous that we can become paralyzed before we even begin.

Maybe God is not asking us to conquer everything we can see.

Maybe he is asking us not to walk past the opportunities to love that he actually places in front of us.

Perhaps we spend too much time searching for some extraordinary way to serve God while stepping over the ordinary opportunities already standing in our path.

The child whose choices disappoint us.

The person we still have not forgiven.

The stranger who needs help.

The money we could share.

The person whose sin is easier to recognize than our own.

The example we quietly set for someone watching us.

And then John gives us the answer: “If we love one another, God remains in us.”

Maybe that is where God becomes visible.

Not necessarily through some enormous act that changes the world, but through hundreds of small decisions in which we choose love over judgment, generosity over wanting, mercy over resentment, and presence over walking away.

We don't have to wake up tomorrow asking, **How am I going to fix everything?**

Perhaps there is only one question we need to carry with us:

**Who has God placed in front of me today, and what would love require of me here?**

That is small enough to begin.

And difficult enough to spend a lifetime learning.
